# Talyn

### Give every task its own agent.

Each session is a branch with its own coding agent, diff and terminal in the cloud. Run as many as you like at once, on the Claude or ChatGPT plan you already have. Each one can open a pull request, and Talyn keeps that pull request green until it merges.

Download · Open in browser · talyn.dev · Docs

Latest release CI License: MIT Platforms

## What Talyn is

Talyn is a desktop and web app for people who hand work to coding agents and then have to land it. [...] ## Get Talyn

 Desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux: GitHub releases or talyn.dev.
 Browser: app.talyn.dev. Same product, same account, nothing to install.

Then sign in, connect GitHub, and connect Claude or ChatGPT when you start your first session. Read the docs for more.

The free plan includes the whole app with a small monthly allowance of box-hours. Prices are on talyn.dev/pricing.

Talyn is in public beta. It works with GitHub only.

 Windows installers are not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen warns on first install.
 The download button on talyn.dev serves the Apple silicon build for macOS. On an Intel Mac, take the x64 build from the releases page.

Talyn is an npm-workspaces monorepo. You need Node.js 18 or newer (22 recommended). [...] Sessions and threads. Parallel agents, each with its own sandbox, branch, diff and terminal.
 Sandboxes. Ready in seconds from an image of your repository. An idle sandbox sleeps after 10 minutes, and a sleeping sandbox is free.
 PR dashboard. My PRs and Reviews, triaged worst first, with a detail sheet for the diff, checks and conversation.
 Fix runs. An agent fixes failing checks, conflicts and review comments and pushes to the same branch.
 Merge queue. Queue a ready PR. If it falls behind or breaks first, an agent fixes it.
 Code review. Several reviewers read a change and a final check drops what it cannot back up. Findings stay in the app unless you post them to GitHub.
 Workflows. Rules for pull request events, such as "when checks fail on a dependency bump, send an agent".

results.title: Breaking Claude Code, Gemini CLI & Codex Sandboxes | Novee
results.content:
We exploited three broken vendor-default containment models: Anthropic’s Claude Code, Google Gemini, OpenAI Codex. Permission rules, process isolation, and kernel enforcement each failed at a different edge of the environment.
 Credentials escaped in every architecture, including from a Codex sandbox with TCP, UDP, and DNS fully disabled.
 The impact includes two Claude Code CVEs (CVE-2026-54316 & CVE-2026-45786), A CVSS 10 Gemini exploit chain from a single public issue to credential compromise and a push to main on software with roughly two million monthly installs, plus two independent Codex sandbox escape paths.
 We tested using the vendors’ official repositories and their own agents with default configurations, confirming this is not a story about a user fumbling their own setup. [...] That’s the job of the harness. It defines the containment policy: deciding what the agent is allowed to touch, with which permissions, and in what environment. It draws a line between what the agent can and cannot do, and that line is the agent sandbox.

We deployed Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex exactly as their vendors ship them, then went looking for the gap between what each sandbox claims to protect and what it actually enforces. We found that gap in all three. Three architectures, all broken.

A sandbox enforces a model of reality, not reality itself, and the exploit lives in whatever that model leaves out. None of these were misconfigurations. In each case a reasonable security decision became unsafe at the edge of what the sandbox could see.

## Key Takeaways [...] One public issue, zero repository privileges, two independent containment failures. The environment gets sanitized; the kernel does not. Google published GHSA-wpqr-6v78-jr5g for the trust and tool-allowlisting failures and scored it CVSS 10.0.

## Round 3: Codex, no network and still an exit

Claude’s software rules had a priority gap, and Gemini’s process boundary leaked through shared kernel state. Codex goes lower still, asking the operating system itself to enforce the boundary.

Codex can run interactively, as an MCP server, or through codex exec – its headless, unattended mode. codex-action wraps codex exec for automation, where no human is available to approve each operation.

That mode still has to decide how much authority the agent gets. Codex exposes three sandbox policies:

results.title: What It Costs to Run Claude Code or Codex in a Cloud Sandbox
results.content:
Running Claude Code with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` belongs in a sandbox, and Anthropic’s documentation says so directly: always run those sessions inside a container, a VM or the sandbox runtime, so that file tools, MCP servers and hooks sit inside the boundary as well.(#src-12) With no prompts, whoever wrote the README, the issue or a dependency’s install script can steer the agent, and what it runs reaches your SSH keys, your cloud credentials and every other repo on your laptop. A cloud sandbox holds none of those. Codex’s `danger-full-access` mode is the same switch, and OpenAI reserves it for isolated environments.(#src-13) [...] You want the agent off your laptop. It might be running with permission prompts turned off, working a ticket while you sit in a meeting, or one of five agents on five branches at once. A cloud sandbox gives each of them its own machine, and the bill turns on a detail most pricing pages bury: whether you pay for the CPU and memory the sandbox reserved, or only for what the agent actually used.

For a coding agent those two numbers are far apart. Claude Code sends a prompt and waits for tokens to stream back, and the builds and test runs between turns are short bursts inside long waits. Every figure below is the sandbox alone; the model usage that drives the agent is a separate bill.

## How Much Does It Cost to Run Claude Code in a Cloud Sandbox? [...] At this scale concurrency bites before price: fifty tickets in flight is fifty sandboxes. E2B’s Hobby plan allows 20 concurrently running sandboxes and Pro allows 100,(#src-2) and Vercel’s Hobby plan allows 10 against 10,000 on Pro.(#src-1) Vercel’s $0.60 per million creations adds under a tenth of a cent.

results.title: Claude Code vs Codex (2026): Comparing the Top Coding Agents | Paradev
results.content:
### Is Claude Code or Codex better?

Both are top-tier. Claude Code is known for deep single-task reliability across many surfaces; Codex for cloud-parallel delegation and OpenAI integration. The best choice depends on your ecosystem, and many teams use both.

### Can I use Claude Code and Codex together?

Yes. They are separate products, and you can run both. A workspace like Paradev runs each as a first-class agent in its own Git worktree, so you can compare them on the same task.

### Do Claude Code or Codex use Git worktrees?

Neither natively isolates parallel tasks in local Git worktrees. Claude Code uses parallel and cloud sessions; Codex uses cloud sandboxes. For a local worktree per task, run them inside a workspace like Paradev. [...] ### Parallelism Model

Neither agent natively gives each parallel task its own local Git worktree. Claude Code offers parallel sessions on the desktop and cloud sessions on the web. Codex leans on isolated cloud environments for parallel tasks. If you want local worktree isolation for parallel work, that comes from a workspace layered on top, not from either agent itself.

### Pricing

Claude Code is bundled with Claude Pro and Max plans and available via the API. Codex is bundled with ChatGPT plans and available via the API. The right value depends on which subscription you already have and your usage; many teams keep both.

### Which Is Better? [...] ## At a Glance

| Claude Code | Codex |
 --- |
| Vendor | Anthropic | OpenAI |
| Surfaces | CLI, desktop, VS Code, JetBrains, web, mobile | CLI, editor, desktop, web, cloud |
| Parallelism | Parallel sessions (desktop); cloud sessions (web) | Isolated cloud environments |
| Local worktree isolation | Not native | Not native (cloud sandboxes instead) |
| Pricing | Claude Pro and Max plans; API | Included with ChatGPT plans; API |
| Best known for | Deep, reliable single-task work | Cloud-parallel task delegation |

results.content:
Run `/run-codex-review review --base main`. Observed errors in the plugin output:

```
failed to write models cache: Read-only file system (os error 30) # ~/.codex/models_cache.json failed to renew cache TTL: Read-only file system (os error 30) bwrap: execvp codex-linux-sandbox: No such file or directory # codex stages its helper into ~/.codex/tmp/arg0/… — blocked 
```

Every internal codex tool call (`git diff`, `ls`, etc.) then fails with `Sandbox(Denied)`, so the review produces no findings — only a failure report. The plugin path (`~/.claude/plugins/data/codex-openai-codex/…`) also isn’t writable, breaking job state logging.

## Root cause
